title: Pierre Gasly stripped of Monaco podium, Isack Hadjar reinstated after FIA court ruling
content:
The 2026 Monaco Grand Prix results have been overturned again, as the FIA International Court of Appeal determined the time penalties initially lodged against Pierre Gasly will stand.

As a result, the Alpine driver lost his podium finish, while Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar regained third place.

The controversial saga dates back to June, when Alpine filed rights of review over the pit lane speeding penalties Gasly received. The Frenchman was not the only driver dealt sanctions for those infringements, but it was later determined the pit lane length was measured incorrectly.

The FIA stewards subsequently determined Gasly had not exceeded the pit lane speed limit, based on the information provided, and overturned his two time penalties. McLaren and Red Bull filed appeals against that move, sending the case to the International Court of Appeal. Alpine and Racing Bulls were also part of the proceedings.

The finalizing point of the proceedings was that the Monaco GP was held with a common parameter that all teams abided by throughout the weekend and made strategic decisions with that speed limit and distance measurement in mind.

“Selectively applying a different post-race parameter to Car 10 would mean that competitors who calibrated and competed against the common benchmark would be judged by one standard,” the court said in its decision, which was published on Friday, “while Car 10 would ultimately be judged by another.”

The court ultimately did not accept the FIA’s explanation that what made Gasly’s decision different from the other competitors is that he did not serve his penalty during the Monaco GP, which allowed for a post-race review to take place.

“A tactical decision concerning when to serve a penalty cannot create for one competitor a different event-wide measurement parameter from that applied to the rest of the field,” it said.

Alpine said in a statement that it is frustrated and disappointed by the court’s decision. It acknowledged the judges’ decision but disagrees, maintaining that Gasly didn’t exceed the pit lane speed limit.

With Gasly dropping from third to seventh, he lost nine points, which impacts Alpine’s constructors’ championship standing. Alpine remains sixth but now faces a 16-point gap to Racing Bulls, with Lawson and Lindblad gaining positions with the decision reversal.

Only one witness was called, Formula One Management’s chief engineering and innovation officer Arbi Karapetian. According to the court’s decision, Karapetian accepted that Gasly would have been below the pit lane speed limit of 60 km/h “only if the actual distance travelled had been less than approximately 2673 cm and 2670 cm respectively,” numbers that represent approximately the distance traveled.

Per the decision, Karapetian “confirmed that he had produced no measurement or other evidence establishing that Car 10 in fact travelled such distances.” This created uncertainty around the Gasly decision, which Alpine could not eliminate with absolute certainty.

The court questioned Alpine, and it revealed it used a CAD model, car data and video imagery to create its “best estimate” of Gasly’s trajectory that day. But it could not guarantee “with any degree of high certainty” that the distance they calculated would be within centimeters of what Gasly actually drove in Monaco.

“The reconstruction therefore did not establish the actual distance travelled by Car 10 in either passage with the precision necessary to resolve the difference between the relevant threshold distances.”

The court also noted how Gasly’s speed limit infractions were higher than the others, which were more in the 0.1 km/h range. And it’s worth remembering that all competitors were judged by the same distance that weekend. McLaren and Red Bull argued that it was “a breach of the equality of treatment and of sporting fairness.”

It was also determined that, technically, the initial distance measurement of 2692cm wasn’t inaccurate but rather, FOM “concluded that, because of the non-perpendicular geometry of the loops, its experienced personnel should have selected a different line.”

The court decided “that once the Official Timekeeper has established and adopted the distance parameter used by the OTS for a Competition, and competitors have been required to calibrate their cars and conduct the Competition by reference to that common parameter, sporting fairness and equal treatment require that the parameter remains fixed for the Competition.”

Essentially, it cannot be retrospectively replaced once an event ends if a different measurement methodology replaces the initial one taken.

The court ultimately felt that Gasly did exceed the speed limit twice and that the stewards erred in their decisions “by rescinding the penalties on the basis of the post-race distance reconstruction.”

The governing body said will review “the methodology and operation of the current Formula 1 timing system and the related regulatory matters,” as well as the “other judicial procedures and operations including the right of review and the appeal processes.”

But as far as the stewarding process is concerned, the FIA “is fully supportive.”
